vignette: The convoy never should have taken that mountain pass. He sits in the driver's seat of a reinforced supply truck, radio crackling with static, when the first explosion tears through the lead vehicle. He remembers the smell of burnt rubber and cordite, the deafening crack that vibrates in his teeth, and the sudden, suffocating silence that follows. He crawls from the cab, shouting names, digging through twisted metal until his hands bleed, only to realize he is the only one walking away. He comes home. He marries the woman he has known for two years, signs the papers for his warehouse, and tries to build a life out of the dust. At fifty-four, he carries himself with the rigid posture of a man who has spent years bracing for impact. His business, a wholesale food distribution company, grows from a single refrigerated unit to a fleet of trucks. He speaks proudly of the cold storage, the route drivers, the contracts with local grocery chains. But the stories always circle back to the pass. His office becomes a series of checkpoints. He checks the security monitors six times an hour. He insists on personally verifying every invoice, even when his accountants assure him the numbers balance. When a delivery truck backfires outside his loading dock, he drops to the floor before his brain can register the sound. His drivers have learned not to call him after six p.m., and he has learned to let the phone ring until it stops. At home, the quiet is his hardest terrain. His wife sets a place for him at the dinner table, but he eats standing up, chewing slowly as if swallowing might trigger something. He wakes at 3:14 a.m. without fail. The ceiling fan sounds like rotor blades. The house settles, and he is back in the pass, pressing his ear to the cold floor, listening for the next detonation. He lies beside his wife, his chest tight, wanting to reach for her hand but afraid that movement might wake the memory. He apologizes the next morning, then apologizes again for leaving her in the dark. Raised in a Latin American household where stoicism was worn as a badge of honor, he never learns the vocabulary for what happens to him. His self-assessment, a PCL-5 that reads sixty-nine, hangs in the room like an unspoken verdict, but he refuses to let it dictate his days. He tells me that he feels like a man wearing a heavy coat in July. He keeps working. He pays his staff on time. He laughs at the occasional joke. But the weight never lifts. It sits in his shoulders, it tightens his jaw when a helicopter flies overhead, it turns the television news into an unwatchable blur. He knows he should rest. He knows he should call it what it is. Instead, he measures his days in inventory counts, in school runs, in the steady rhythm of a life he is determined to keep moving forward, even though the map he is following no longer matches the terrain. He watches the street again. A delivery van pulls into the lot below. He exhales. He waits for the next sound.
